chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter I
paragraphs: Early in 1806, Nicholas Rostov returned home on leave. Denisov was heading to Voronezh, and Rostov convinced him to travel together as far as Moscow and stay with him there. At the last post station before Moscow, Denisov had drunk three bottles of wine with a fellow officer and, despite the jolting ride over the rutted, snow-covered road, slept the entire way, lying at the bottom of the sleigh beside Rostov, who grew more and more impatient as they neared the city.

"How much farther? How much longer? These unbearable streets, shops, bakery signs, street lamps, and sleighs!" Rostov thought, after their travel permits had been checked at the city gate and they had entered Moscow.
"Denisov! We're here! He's asleep," he added, leaning his whole body forward as if that might somehow make the sleigh go faster.
Denisov didn't answer.

"There's the corner where the cabman Zakhar has his stand — and there's Zakhar himself, with the same old horse! And there's the little shop where we used to buy gingerbread! Can't you go faster? Come on!"
"Which house?" asked the driver.
"That one, right at the end, the big one. Can't you see? That's our house," said Rostov. "Of course it's our house! Denisov, Denisov! We're almost there!"
Denisov lifted his head, coughed, and said nothing.
"Dmitri," said Rostov to his servant on the box, "those lights are in our house, aren't they?"
"Yes, sir, and there's a light on in your father's study."

"So they haven't gone to bed yet! Good. And don't forget to put out my new coat," added Rostov, fingering his new mustache. "Now hurry up," he shouted to the driver. "Wake up, Vaska!" he said, turning to Denisov, whose head was nodding again. "Come on, get moving! I'll give you three rubles for vodka — just go!" Rostov shouted when the sleigh was only three houses from his door. It felt as though the horses had stopped moving entirely. At last the sleigh turned right, pulled up at an entrance, and Rostov looked up to see the old familiar cornice with its bit of chipped plaster, the porch, and the post beside the pavement. He leaped out before the sleigh had stopped and ran into the hall. The house was cold and quiet, as if it didn't care who had come to it. There was no one in the hall. "Oh God! Is everyone all right?" he thought, pausing for a moment with a sinking heart, then immediately running through the hall and up the worn, familiar staircase. The old door handle — the one that always annoyed the countess when it wasn't properly cleaned — turned as loosely as ever. A single tallow candle burned in the anteroom.

Old Mikhail was asleep on the chest. Prokofy the footman, who was so strong he could lift the back of a carriage by himself, sat braiding slippers from cloth scraps. He looked up when the door opened, and his expression of sleepy indifference instantly transformed into delighted amazement.

"Good heavens! The young count!" he cried, recognizing his young master. "Can it be? My dear boy!" And Prokofy, trembling with excitement, rushed toward the drawing room door — probably to announce him — but then changed his mind, came back, and bent down to kiss the young man's shoulder.
"Everyone well?" asked Rostov, pulling his arm away.
"Yes, thank God! Yes! They've just finished supper. Let me look at you, your excellency."
"Everything's really all right?"
"Yes, thank the Lord!"

Rostov, who had completely forgotten about Denisov and not wanting anyone to get there before him, threw off his fur coat and ran on tiptoe through the large, dark ballroom. Everything was the same: the same old card tables, the same chandelier with its dust cover. But someone had already spotted the young master, and before he reached the drawing room, something burst from a side door like a whirlwind and started hugging and kissing him. Then another creature of the same kind flew out from a second door, and a third — more hugging, more kissing, more shouts and tears of joy. He couldn't tell who was Papa, who was Natasha, and who was Petya. Everyone shouted, talked, and kissed him all at once. Only his mother was not among them, he noticed.
"I didn't know... Nicholas... My darling!..."
"Here he is... our own boy... Kolya, sweetheart... How he's changed!... Where are the candles?... Tea!..."
* Kolya is the familiar form of Nicholas.
"And me — kiss me!"
"Darling... and me!"
Sonya, Natasha, Petya, Anna Mikhaylovna, Vera, and the old count were all hugging him, while the servants — men and women alike — crowded into the room, exclaiming and gasping.
Petya clung to his legs, shouting, "And me too!"
Natasha, after pulling him down toward her and covering his face with kisses while gripping the hem of his coat, sprang away and began prancing in place like a goat, letting out a piercing shriek.
All around him were loving eyes glistening with tears of joy, and everywhere were lips seeking a kiss.

Sonya too, her face flushed pink, clung to his arm and gazed at him, radiant with happiness, eagerly waiting for the look she longed for. She was sixteen now and very pretty, especially at this moment of joyful, rapturous excitement. She stared at him without blinking, smiling and holding her breath. He gave her a grateful look but was still searching for someone. The old countess hadn't come yet. Then footsteps were heard at the door — footsteps so rapid they could hardly be his mother's.

Yet it was her, wearing a new dress he didn't recognize, made after he had left. Everyone else let go of him, and he ran to her. When they met, she fell against his chest, sobbing. She couldn't lift her face — she just pressed it against the cold braiding of his hussar jacket. Denisov, who had entered the room unnoticed, stood there and wiped his eyes at the sight.
"Vasili Denisov, your son's friend," he said, introducing himself to the count, who was looking at him questioningly.
"Welcome! Most welcome! I know, I know," said the count, kissing and embracing Denisov. "Nicholas wrote us about you... Natasha, Vera — look! Here is Denisov!"
The same happy, glowing faces turned toward Denisov's shaggy figure.

"Dear Denisov!" screamed Natasha, beside herself with joy, springing toward him, throwing her arms around him, and kissing him. This display made everyone feel a bit awkward. Denisov blushed too, but smiled, took Natasha's hand, and kissed it.
Denisov was shown to his room, and the Rostovs all gathered around Nicholas in the sitting room.

The old countess, refusing to let go of his hand and kissing it every other moment, sat beside him. The rest crowded around, watching his every movement, word, and expression, never taking their adoring eyes off him. His brother and sisters jostled for the spots closest to him and argued over who would bring him his tea, his handkerchief, his pipe.

Rostov was deeply happy in the love they showed him, but the first moment of reunion had been so perfect that now his joy seemed insufficient, and he kept expecting something more — more and still more.
The next morning, after the fatigue of their journey, the travelers slept until ten o'clock.

In the room next to their bedroom lay a jumble of sabers, satchels, sword belts, open trunks, and dirty boots. Two freshly cleaned pairs with spurs had just been set against the wall. Servants brought in pitchers and basins, hot water for shaving, and well-brushed clothes. The room smelled of men and tobacco.
"Hey, Grishka — my pipe!" came Denisov's husky voice. "Rostov, get up!"
Rostov, rubbing his eyes, which seemed glued shut, lifted his tousled head from the warm pillow.
"Is it late?"

"Late! It's nearly ten o'clock," answered Natasha's voice. A rustle of starched petticoats and the whispering and laughter of girls came from the next room. The door cracked open and there was a glimpse of something blue — ribbons, dark hair, and cheerful faces. It was Natasha, Sonya, and Petya, who had come to check if they were up yet.
"Nicholas! Get up!" Natasha's voice came again at the door.
"Coming!"

Meanwhile Petya, who had found the sabers in the outer room, seized them with a boy's natural delight at anything military. Forgetting that it wasn't proper for the girls to see men undressed, he threw open the bedroom door.
"Is this your saber?" he shouted.

The girls jumped aside. Denisov hid his hairy legs under the blanket and looked with a panicked face at his comrade for help. The door, having let Petya in, closed again. Laughter erupted from behind it.
"Nicholas! Come out in your dressing gown!" called Natasha's voice.
"Is this your saber?" asked Petya. "Or is it yours?" he added, turning to the dark-mustached Denisov with exaggerated respect.

Rostov hurriedly pulled on something for his feet, threw on his dressing gown, and came out. Natasha had put on one spurred boot and was trying to get her foot into the other. Sonya was twirling around, about to puff out her skirts like a balloon and sit down. They were both wearing identical new pale-blue dresses, and both looked fresh, rosy, and bright. Sonya ran off, but Natasha took her brother's arm and led him to the sitting room, where they started talking. They barely gave each other time to ask questions and get answers about a thousand small things that could only matter to the two of them. Natasha laughed at everything he said and everything she said — not because any of it was funny, but because she was happy and couldn't contain her joy, which came out as laughter.
"Oh, how lovely! How wonderful!" she said to everything.

Rostov felt that under the influence of the warm glow of love, the childlike smile that had not appeared on his face once since he left home now returned for the first time in eighteen months, brightening both his soul and his face.
"No, but listen," she said, "you're really a grown man now, aren't you? I'm so glad you're my brother." She touched his mustache. "I want to know what you men are like. Are you the same as us? No?"
"Why did Sonya run away?" asked Rostov.
"Oh, that's a whole long story! How are you going to talk to her — formally or informally?"
"However it happens," said Rostov.
"No, use the formal 'you,' please! I'll tell you all about it another time. Actually, I'll tell you now. You know Sonya is my dearest friend. Such a close friend that I burned my arm for her. Look!"
She pushed up her muslin sleeve and showed him a red scar on her long, slender arm, high above the elbow — a spot normally covered even by a ball gown.
"I burned this to prove my love for her. I just heated a ruler over a candle and pressed it right there!"

Sitting on the sofa with the little cushions on its arms, in what had been his old schoolroom, looking into Natasha's wildly bright eyes, Rostov re-entered that world of home and childhood that meant nothing to anyone else but gave him some of the greatest joys of his life. Burning one's arm with a ruler to prove love didn't seem senseless to him — he understood it and wasn't surprised by it at all.
"And that's all?" he asked.

"We're such friends, such close friends! All that ruler business was just silliness, but we're friends forever. When she loves someone, she does it for life — but I'm not like that. I forget quickly."
"So what then?"
"She loves me, and she loves you the same way."
Natasha suddenly blushed.

"She says you should forget all about what happened before you left.... She says, 'I will always love him, but let him be free.' Isn't that beautiful and noble? Yes, really noble — isn't it?" asked Natasha, so seriously and passionately that it was clear she had discussed this before, with tears.
Rostov grew thoughtful.
"I never go back on my word," he said. "Besides, Sonya is so lovely that only a fool would give up such happiness."

"No, no!" cried Natasha. "She and I have already talked about this. We knew you'd say that. But it won't work, because if you say it like that — if you act like you're bound by your promise — then it seems as though she wasn't being sincere. It would make it look like you're marrying her out of obligation, and that's no good at all."

Rostov saw that they had thought this through carefully. Sonya had already struck him with her beauty the day before. Today, having caught a glimpse of her, she seemed even lovelier. She was a charming sixteen-year-old girl, obviously passionately in love with him — he didn't doubt that for a moment. Why shouldn't he love her now, and even marry her? But at the moment, there were so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him! "Yes, they've made a wise decision," he thought. "I should stay free."
"Well then, that's perfect," he said. "We'll talk about it later. Oh, how glad I am to have you!"
"So — are you still faithful to Boris?" he continued.
"Oh, what nonsense!" cried Natasha, laughing. "I don't think about him or anyone else, and I don't want any of that."
"Really! So what are you up to these days?"
"These days?" repeated Natasha, and a happy smile lit up her face. "Have you seen Duport?"
"No."
"You haven't seen Duport — the famous dancer? Well then, you won't understand. That's what I'm up to."

Curving her arms and holding out her skirts like a ballerina, Natasha backed up a few steps, spun around, performed a little jump, clicked her feet sharply together, and rose up on the very tips of her toes.
"See? I'm standing! See!" she said, but couldn't hold herself on her toes any longer. "So that's what I'm doing! I'll never marry anyone — I'm going to be a dancer. But don't tell anyone."
Rostov laughed so loudly and joyfully that Denisov in the bedroom felt a pang of envy, and Natasha couldn't help joining in.
"Don't you think it's wonderful?" she kept repeating.
"Wonderful! And so you don't want to marry Boris anymore?"
Natasha flared up. "I don't want to marry anyone. And I'll tell him so myself when I see him!"
"Goodness!" said Rostov.
"But that's all silly," Natasha chattered on. "Is Denisov nice?" she asked.
"Very nice."
"Well then — goodbye. Go get dressed. Is he very scary, Denisov?"
"Why scary?" asked Nicholas. "No, Vaska is a wonderful fellow."
"You call him Vaska? That's funny! Is he really nice?"
"Very."
"All right then, hurry up. We'll all have breakfast together."

And Natasha rose and tiptoed out of the room like a ballerina, but with the kind of smile that only happy fifteen-year-old girls can manage. When Rostov met Sonya in the drawing room, he blushed. He didn't know how to behave around her. The night before, in the first joyful moment of reunion, they had kissed. But today that felt impossible. He sensed that everyone — his mother, his sisters, all of them — was watching him, waiting to see how he would act with her. He kissed her hand and addressed her formally. But their eyes met and spoke intimately, exchanging tender, silent kisses. Her gaze asked forgiveness for having dared, through Natasha, to remind him of his promise — and thanked him for his love. His gaze thanked her for offering him his freedom and told her that one way or another, he would never stop loving her, because that would be impossible.
"How strange," said Vera, choosing a moment when everyone was silent, "that Sonya and Nicholas now address each other formally and act like strangers."

Vera's observation was accurate, as her remarks always were. But like most of her comments, it made everyone uncomfortable — not just Sonya, Nicholas, and Natasha, but even the old countess, who dreaded this love affair that might prevent Nicholas from making a brilliant match. She blushed like a young girl.

Denisov, to Rostov's surprise, appeared in the drawing room with pomaded hair, wearing cologne and a new uniform, looking as sharp as he made himself before going into battle. He was more charming with the ladies and gentlemen than Rostov had ever seen him.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter II
paragraphs: After returning to Moscow from the army, Nicholas Rostov was welcomed by his household as the best of sons, a hero, and their darling Nikolenka; by his relatives as a charming, attractive, and well-mannered young man; and by his acquaintances as a handsome hussar lieutenant, a good dancer, and one of the best catches in the city.

The Rostovs knew everyone in Moscow. The old count had enough money that year, since all his estates had been remortgaged, so Nicholas — having acquired his own racing horse, the most fashionable riding breeches (a style no one else in Moscow had yet), and the latest boots with sharply pointed toes and small silver spurs — had a very good time. After a short period of readjusting to civilian life, Nicholas found it quite pleasant to be home again. He felt that he had grown up and matured considerably. His old despair over failing a Scripture exam, borrowing money from Gavril to pay a sleigh driver, secretly kissing Sonya — he now looked back on all of it as childishness he had left far behind. Now he was a lieutenant of hussars in a silver-braided jacket, wearing the Cross of St. George — a medal awarded for bravery in combat — and he was training a racing horse with well-known, older, respected horsemen. He had a lady acquaintance on one of the boulevards whom he visited in the evenings. He led the mazurka at the Arkharovs' ball, discussed the war with Field Marshal Kamenski, frequented the English Club, and was on friendly terms with a forty-year-old colonel to whom Denisov had introduced him.

His passion for the Emperor had cooled somewhat in Moscow. Still, since he didn't see him and had no opportunity to, he often spoke about him and about his devotion, hinting that he hadn't told everything — that there was something in his feelings for the Emperor that not everyone could understand. With his whole heart he shared the adoration then common in Moscow for the Emperor, who was referred to as "the angel incarnate."

During Rostov's short stay in Moscow before returning to the army, he didn't grow closer to Sonya — if anything, he drifted away from her. She was very pretty and sweet, and clearly deeply in love with him, but he was at that age when there seems to be so much to do that there's no time for love, and a young man values his freedom, which he needs for so many other things. When he thought of Sonya, he told himself, "There will be plenty of girls like her — girls I haven't even met yet. There'll be time enough to think about love when I want to, but right now I have no time." Besides, the company of women struck him as somehow beneath his manhood. He went to balls and into ladies' society while making a show of doing it reluctantly. The races, the English Club, drinking bouts with Denisov, and visits to a certain house — that was a different matter entirely, and perfectly fitting for a dashing young hussar!
At the beginning of March, old Count Ilya Rostov was consumed with arranging a dinner in honor of Prince Bagration at the English Club.

The count paced the hall in his dressing gown, issuing orders to the club steward and to the famous Feoktist, the club's head chef, about asparagus, fresh cucumbers, strawberries, veal, and fish for the dinner. The count had been a founding member and committee member of the club. They had entrusted him with organizing the Bagration celebration because few people knew how to put on a lavish, generous feast like he did, and fewer still would be as willing and able to cover shortfalls from their own pocket. The chef and steward listened to his orders with pleased expressions, knowing that under no other management could they so easily skim a handsome profit from a dinner costing several thousand rubles.
"Now remember — cocks' combs in the turtle soup, you hear!"
"Three cold dishes, then?" asked the chef.
The count considered.
"Can't have fewer — yes, three... The mayonnaise, that's one," he said, counting on his fingers.
"Should I order those large sterlets?" asked the steward.

"Yes, we'll have to — they won't sell them for less. Oh dear, I almost forgot — we need another side dish. Good heavens!" he clutched his head. "Who's going to get me the flowers? Dmitri! Hey, Dmitri! Run out to our Moscow estate," he said to the factotum who appeared at his call. "Hurry up and tell Maksim the gardener to put the servants to work. Everything from the hothouses must be brought here, wrapped carefully in felt. I need two hundred pots here by Friday."

After giving several more orders, he was about to go see his "little countess" for a rest when he remembered something else important. He came back, called the chef and steward again, and resumed giving directions. Light footsteps and the clink of spurs sounded at the door, and the young count walked in — handsome, rosy-cheeked, with a dark little mustache, visibly rested and looking sleeker from his comfortable Moscow life.

"Ah, my boy, my head's spinning!" said the old man with a smile, looking slightly embarrassed in front of his son. "If only you'd help a little! I need singers too. I'll have my own orchestra, but should we also bring in the gypsy singers? You military types like that sort of thing."
"Really, Papa, I think Prince Bagration worried less before the Battle of Schon Grabern than you're worrying now," said his son with a smile.
The old count pretended to be offended.
"Easy for you to say — try doing it yourself!"
And the count turned to the chef, who watched the father and son with a shrewd, respectful, and sympathetic expression.
"What are young people coming to these days, eh, Feoktist?" he said. "Laughing at us old fellows!"
"That's right, your excellency. All they have to do is eat a good dinner — but putting it all together and serving it, that's not their department!"

"Exactly!" exclaimed the count, and cheerfully seizing his son by both hands, he cried, "Now I've got you! Take the sleigh and pair right away and go to Bezukhov's. Tell him Count Ilya sent you to ask for strawberries and fresh pineapples. We can't get them from anyone else. He's not there himself, so you'll have to go in and ask the princesses. And from there, head to Razgulyay — the coachman Ipatka knows the way — and find the gypsy Ilyushka, the one who danced at Count Orlov's in a white Cossack coat, and bring him to me."
"And should I bring the gypsy girls along too?" asked Nicholas, laughing. "Oh, dear..."

At that moment, with quiet footsteps and the businesslike, preoccupied, yet meekly pious expression that never left her face, Anna Mikhaylovna entered the hall. Though she found the count in his dressing gown every day, he always became flustered and apologized for his appearance.

"Not at all, my dear count," she said, modestly lowering her eyes. "But I'll go to Bezukhov's myself. Pierre has arrived, and now we can get whatever we need from his hothouses. I need to see him anyway. He's forwarded me a letter from Boris. Thank God, Boris is now on the staff."
The count was delighted that Anna Mikhaylovna was taking one of his errands off his hands, and he ordered the small closed carriage for her.
"Tell Bezukhov to come. I'll put his name on the list. Is his wife with him?" he asked.
Anna Mikhaylovna raised her eyes to the ceiling, and an expression of deep sorrow crossed her face.

"Oh, my dear friend, his situation is very unfortunate," she said. "If what we hear is true, it's terrible. How little we imagined such a thing when we were celebrating his happiness! And such a pure, angelic soul as young Bezukhov! Yes, I feel for him deeply and will try to offer what comfort I can."
"What — what's happened?" asked both the young and old Rostov.
Anna Mikhaylovna sighed deeply.

"Dolokhov — Maria Ivanovna's son," she said in a conspiratorial whisper, "has completely compromised her, they say. Pierre took him in, invited him to stay at his house in Petersburg, and now... she's come here, and that daredevil followed her!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, intending to show sympathy for Pierre, but betraying through her tone and a half-smile that her sympathies lay partly with the "daredevil," as she called Dolokhov. "They say Pierre is absolutely devastated."
"Dear, dear! Still, tell him to come to the club — it'll all blow over. It's going to be an incredible banquet."

The next day, March third, shortly after one o'clock, two hundred and fifty members of the English Club and fifty guests were waiting for the guest of honor and hero of the Austrian campaign, Prince Bagration, to arrive for dinner.

When news of the Battle of Austerlitz first reached Moscow, the city had been stunned. Russians were so accustomed to victories that when they heard of the defeat, some simply refused to believe it, while others searched for some extraordinary explanation. At the English Club — where everyone distinguished, important, and well-informed gathered — when the news began arriving in December, no one spoke about the war or the battle, as though everyone had agreed to stay silent. The men who set the tone in conversation — Count Rostopchin, Prince Yuri Dolgorukov, Valuev, Count Markov, and Prince Vyazemski — stopped coming to the club, meeting instead in private homes and intimate circles. Muscovites who took their cues from others — Ilya Rostov among them — were left without a clear opinion on the war and without leaders. Everyone felt that something was terribly wrong, and that discussing bad news was difficult, so silence seemed best. But after a while, like a jury emerging from deliberation, the opinion-makers reappeared, and everyone began speaking clearly and with conviction. Explanations were found for the incredible, unprecedented, and seemingly impossible event of a Russian defeat, and the same conclusions began circulating in every corner of Moscow. The causes were: Austrian treachery, a failing supply chain, the treachery of the Pole Przhebyshevski and the Frenchman Langeron, Kutuzov's incompetence, and — whispered quietly — the youth and inexperience of the Emperor, who had trusted worthless and insignificant advisers. But the army itself, the Russian army, everyone declared, had been extraordinary and had performed miracles of bravery. The soldiers, officers, and generals were all heroes. But the greatest hero of all was Prince Bagration, who had distinguished himself at Schon Grabern and during the retreat from Austerlitz, where he alone had withdrawn his column intact, holding off an enemy force twice his own size for an entire day. What also made Bagration Moscow's hero of choice was that he had no connections in the city and was a stranger there. In honoring him, they were paying tribute to a simple fighting Russian soldier without political connections or intrigues — a man associated through the Italian campaign with the great name of Suvorov. Moreover, celebrating Bagration was the perfect way to express disapproval of Kutuzov.

"If there had been no Bagration, it would have been necessary to invent him," said the wit Shinshin, riffing on Voltaire. No one spoke of Kutuzov except a few who cursed him in whispers, calling him a court weathervane and a dirty old man.

All Moscow repeated Prince Dolgorukov's quip: "If you keep kneading and kneading, you're bound to get your hands dirty" — offering the consolation of past victories to soften the present defeat. People also quoted Rostopchin's observation that French soldiers need lofty speeches to drive them into battle, Germans need logical arguments proving it's more dangerous to run away than to advance, but Russian soldiers simply need to be held back. Everywhere, new stories circulated about individual acts of heroism by Russian officers and soldiers at Austerlitz. One man had saved a regimental standard, another had killed five Frenchmen, a third had loaded five cannons single-handedly. People who didn't know Berg personally told how he had taken his sword in his left hand after being wounded in the right, and pressed forward. Of Bolkonsky, nothing was said, and only those who knew him personally mourned that he had died so young, leaving behind a pregnant wife and an eccentric father.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter III
paragraphs: On that third of March, every room of the English Club buzzed with conversation, like bees swarming in spring. Members and guests wandered back and forth, sitting, standing, meeting, and separating — some in uniform, some in evening dress, and a few wearing powdered wigs and old-fashioned Russian kaftans. Powdered footmen in livery with buckled shoes and smart stockings stood at every door, anxiously tracking every visitor's movement so they could offer their services. Most of those present were elderly, respectable men with broad, self-assured faces, thick fingers, and decisive gestures and voices. This class of guests and members occupied their usual seats and gathered in their usual groups. A smaller portion were casual visitors — mostly young men, including Denisov, Rostov, and Dolokhov, who was now once again an officer in the Semenov regiment. The faces of these younger men, especially the military ones, wore an expression of polite condescension toward their elders that seemed to say, "We're happy to respect and honor you, but remember — the future belongs to us."

Nesvitski was there as a longtime club member. Pierre, who at his wife's insistence had let his hair grow and given up his spectacles, moved through the rooms in fashionable clothes but looking sad and listless. Here, as everywhere, he was surrounded by an atmosphere of deference to his wealth, and being accustomed to dominating such people, he treated them with distracted contempt.

By age he should have belonged to the younger set, but his wealth and connections placed him among the older, more distinguished guests, so he drifted from group to group. Some of the most prominent older men formed the centers of circles that even strangers approached respectfully to hear. The largest groups surrounded Count Rostopchin, Valuev, and Naryshkin. Rostopchin was describing how the Russians had been overrun by fleeing Austrians and had to cut through them with bayonets.
Valuev was confiding that Uvarov had been sent from Petersburg to find out what Moscow was thinking about Austerlitz.

In a third circle, Naryshkin was telling the story of how Suvorov had crowed like a rooster at an Austrian war council in response to the nonsense the Austrian generals were spouting. Shinshin, standing nearby, tried to crack a joke — saying Kutuzov had clearly failed to learn even that simple trick from Suvorov — but the senior members gave the wit a stern look, making him understand that in this place and on this occasion, it was inappropriate to speak that way about Kutuzov.

Count Ilya Rostov, hurried and preoccupied, bustled about in his soft-soled shoes between the dining room and drawing room, greeting important and unimportant guests alike — all of whom he knew — as if they were all equals, while his eyes kept searching for his fine, well-built young son, resting on him and winking at him happily. Young Rostov stood at a window with Dolokhov, whom he had recently met and whose company he greatly valued. The old count approached them and shook Dolokhov's hand.

"Please come visit us... you know my brave boy here... you were out there together... both playing the hero... Ah, Vasili Ignatovich... How are you, old friend?" he said, turning to a passing elderly man. But before he could finish his greeting, a general commotion broke out and a footman rushed in with a frightened face to announce: "He's arrived!"

Bells rang, the stewards hurried forward, and the guests — who had been scattered through different rooms like grain tossed in a shovel — poured together and crowded into the large drawing room by the ballroom entrance.

Bagration appeared in the anteroom doorway, without his hat or sword, which he had left with the porter as club custom required. He wore no lambskin cap and carried no loaded whip over his shoulder, as when Rostov had seen him on the eve of Austerlitz. Instead he wore a crisp new uniform with Russian and foreign decorations and the Star of St. George on his left breast. He had clearly just had his hair and whiskers trimmed for the occasion, which actually made him look slightly worse. There was something innocently festive about his appearance that, combined with his strong, masculine features, gave him a rather comical look. Bekleshev and Theodore Uvarov, who had arrived with him, paused at the doorway to let him enter first as guest of honor. Bagration was embarrassed by the courtesy and reluctant to accept it, which caused a brief delay at the door — but eventually he did enter first. He walked shyly and awkwardly across the parquet floor of the reception room, unsure what to do with his hands. He was far more comfortable walking across a plowed field under fire, as he had done leading the Kursk regiment at Schon Grabern — that would have been easier. The committee members met him at the first door and, expressing their delight at receiving such a distinguished guest, took charge of him without waiting for a reply, surrounded him, and led him to the drawing room. At first it was impossible to get through the drawing room door because of the crowd of members and guests jostling one another, each trying to get a good look at Bagration over the heads in front of them, as if he were some rare creature. Count Ilya Rostov, laughing and repeating, "Make way, my dear! Make way!" pushed through the crowd more energetically than anyone, led the guests into the drawing room, and seated them on the center sofa. The most important men and most respected members pressed around the new arrivals. Count Ilya pushed through the crowd again, left the drawing room, and returned a moment later with another committee member, carrying a large silver tray that he presented to Prince Bagration. On the tray lay verses composed and printed in the hero's honor. Bagration, seeing the tray, looked around in alarm as if searching for help. But every face demanded that he accept. He firmly took the tray with both hands and looked sternly, almost reproachfully, at the count who had presented it. Someone helpfully took the platter from him — otherwise he seemed prepared to carry it all evening and walk into dinner with it — and drew his attention to the verses.

"Very well, I'll read them then!" Bagration seemed to say, and fixing his weary eyes on the paper, he began reading with a fixed, serious expression. But the author himself took the verses and started reading them aloud. Bagration bowed his head and listened:

Bring glory then to Alexander's reign / And on the throne our Titus shield. / A dreaded foe be thou, kindhearted as a man, / A Rhipheus at home, a Caesar in the field! / E'en fortunate Napoleon / Knows by experience, now, Bagration, / And dare not Herculean Russians trouble...
But before the reading was finished, a booming major-domo announced that dinner was served! The door opened, and from the dining room came the resounding strains of a polonaise:
Conquest's joyful thunder waken, / Triumph, valiant Russians, now!...

Count Rostov, glancing irritably at the author who was still reading his verses, bowed to Bagration. Everyone stood, recognizing that dinner mattered more than poetry, and Bagration once again led the way in. He was seated in the place of honor between two men named Alexander — Bekleshev and Naryshkin — a meaningful nod to the Emperor's name. Three hundred people took their seats according to rank and importance, the most distinguished sitting closest to the guest of honor, as naturally as water flows to the lowest ground.

Just before dinner, Count Ilya Rostov introduced his son to Bagration, who recognized him and said a few words — halting and awkward, like everything he said that day. Count Ilya beamed with pride as Bagration spoke to his son.

Nicholas Rostov sat with Denisov and his new acquaintance Dolokhov near the middle of the table. Across from them sat Pierre, next to Prince Nesvitski. Count Ilya Rostov, along with the other committee members, sat facing Bagration and, as the very embodiment of Moscow hospitality, served as the prince's host.

His efforts had not been wasted. The dinner — both the Lenten dishes and the regular fare — was magnificent, yet he couldn't relax until the meal was over. He kept winking at the butler, whispering instructions to the footmen, and awaiting each course with visible anxiety. Everything was superb. With the second course, an enormous sterlet — the sight of which made Ilya Rostov blush with self-conscious pleasure — the footmen began popping champagne corks and filling glasses. After the fish, which caused quite a stir, the count exchanged looks with the other committee members. "There'll be many toasts — it's time to start," he whispered, and raising his glass, he stood up. Everyone fell silent, waiting for what he would say.

"To the health of our Sovereign, the Emperor!" he cried, and at that moment his kind eyes glistened with tears of joy and emotion. The band instantly struck up "Conquest's joyful thunder waken..." Everyone rose and shouted "Hurrah!" Bagration also stood and shouted "Hurrah!" in exactly the same voice he had used on the battlefield at Schon Grabern. Young Rostov's ecstatic voice rang out above the three hundred others. He nearly wept. "To the health of our Sovereign, the Emperor!" he roared, "Hurrah!" He drained his glass in one gulp and smashed it on the floor. Many followed his example, and the loud cheering went on for a long time. When the noise died down, the footmen swept away the broken glass and everyone sat down again, smiling at the racket they had made and exchanging remarks. The old count stood up again, glanced at a note beside his plate, and proposed another toast: "To the health of the hero of our last campaign, Prince Pyotr Ivanovich Bagration!" His blue eyes filled with tears once more. "Hurrah!" the three hundred voices cried again. But this time, instead of the band, a choir began singing a cantata composed by Pavel Ivanovich Kutuzov:
Russians! O'er all barriers on! / Courage conquest guarantees; / Have we not Bagration? / He brings foemen to their knees...

As soon as the singing ended, one toast followed another. Count Ilya Rostov grew more and more emotional, more glasses were smashed, and the cheering grew louder. They drank to Bekleshev, Naryshkin, Uvarov, Dolgorukov, Apraksin, Valuev, the committee, all the club members, and all the club guests — and finally to Count Ilya Rostov himself, as the organizer of the banquet. At that toast, the count pulled out his handkerchief, covered his face, and wept openly.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Pierre sat across from Dolokhov and Nicholas Rostov. As usual, he ate and drank heavily. But those who knew him well could see that some great change had come over him that day. He was silent throughout dinner, looking around while blinking and frowning, or else staring into space with complete absent-mindedness, rubbing the bridge of his nose. His face was gloomy and troubled. He seemed to see and hear nothing happening around him, entirely absorbed by some painful, unresolved problem.

The problem tormenting him had been set in motion by hints from the princess — his cousin — in Moscow, regarding Dolokhov's intimacy with his wife, and by an anonymous letter he had received that morning. The letter, written in the typically crude and mocking style of such messages, said that he couldn't see well through his spectacles, but that his wife's affair with Dolokhov was a secret to no one but him. Pierre categorically refused to believe either the princess's hints or the letter, but he now dreaded looking at Dolokhov, who sat right across from him. Every time he accidentally met Dolokhov's handsome, insolent eyes, Pierre felt something terrible and monstrous rising in his soul and quickly turned away. Involuntarily recalling his wife's past and her relationship with Dolokhov, Pierre could see clearly that what the letter described might be true — or at least could appear true — if it hadn't been about his own wife. He couldn't help remembering how Dolokhov, who had fully recovered his former standing after the campaign, had returned to Petersburg and come to him. Taking advantage of their friendship as drinking companions, Dolokhov had moved straight into Pierre's house, and Pierre had put him up and lent him money. Pierre recalled how Helene had smiled disapprovingly at Dolokhov living with them, and how Dolokhov had brazenly complimented Pierre on his wife's beauty — and from that point on, all the way to Moscow, had never left them for a single day.

"Yes, he's very handsome," thought Pierre, "and I know his character. It would give him special pleasure to dishonor my name and humiliate me, precisely because I've gone out of my way for him — befriended him, helped him. I know and understand how much extra relish that would add to the pleasure of deceiving me, if it were really true. Yes, if it were true — but I don't believe it. I have no right to believe it, and I can't." He remembered the expression Dolokhov's face took on in moments of cruelty — when he had tied a policeman to a bear and dropped them into the water, when he had challenged a man to a duel for no reason, when he had shot a coachman's horse with a pistol. That expression was often on Dolokhov's face when he looked at Pierre. "Yes, he's a thug," thought Pierre. "Killing a man means nothing to him. He must think everyone's afraid of him, and that must please him. He probably thinks I'm afraid of him too — and in fact, I am." And again he felt something terrible and monstrous rising within him. Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov were sitting across from Pierre and seemed to be in high spirits. Rostov was talking cheerfully with his two friends — one a dashing hussar, the other a notorious duelist and libertine — and he kept glancing mockingly at Pierre, whose preoccupied, distracted, and massive figure was quite conspicuous at the dinner. Rostov regarded Pierre with hostility — first, because in a hussar's eyes Pierre was merely a rich civilian married to a beauty, in other words, an old woman; and second, because Pierre, lost in his own thoughts, hadn't recognized Rostov or returned his greeting. When the toast to the Emperor's health was drunk, Pierre, deep in thought, didn't stand or raise his glass.
"What are you doing?" shouted Rostov, staring at him in an ecstasy of indignation. "Don't you hear? It's His Majesty the Emperor's health!"
Pierre sighed, stood up obediently, emptied his glass, and after everyone had sat down again, turned to Rostov with his usual kind smile.
"I'm sorry — I didn't recognize you!" he said. But Rostov was already occupied with something else — he was shouting "Hurrah!"
"Why don't you go reintroduce yourself?" said Dolokhov to Rostov.
"Forget him — he's an idiot," said Rostov.
"One should make an effort with the husbands of pretty women," said Denisov.
Pierre didn't catch what they were saying, but he knew they were talking about him. He turned red and looked away.
"Well then — to the health of beautiful women!" said Dolokhov, and with a serious expression but a smile lurking at the corners of his mouth, he raised his glass toward Pierre.
"To the health of lovely women, my dear Petrusha — and their lovers!" he added.

Pierre, eyes downcast, drained his glass without looking at Dolokhov or responding. A footman distributing copies of Kutuzov's cantata placed one in front of Pierre as one of the principal guests. He was about to pick it up when Dolokhov leaned across the table and snatched it from his hand, starting to read it. Pierre stared at Dolokhov, and his eyes darkened. The terrible, monstrous thing that had been tormenting him all through dinner surged up and took hold of him. He heaved his massive body across the table.
"How dare you take that!" he shouted.
Hearing that shout and seeing who it was directed at, Nesvitski and the man sitting beside Pierre turned to him in alarm.
"Stop! Stop! What are you doing?" came their frightened whispers.
Dolokhov looked at Pierre with clear, amused, cruel eyes, wearing that smile of his that seemed to say, "Ah, now this is what I enjoy."
"You won't have it," he said distinctly.
Pierre, white-faced, his lips trembling, grabbed the copy back.
"You... you... scoundrel! I challenge you!" he burst out, and shoving back his chair, he rose from the table.

At the very instant he said those words, Pierre felt that the question of his wife's guilt — which had been torturing him all day — was finally and conclusively answered: yes, she was guilty. He hated her and was forever separated from her. Despite Denisov's plea that he stay out of it, Rostov agreed to serve as Dolokhov's second. After dinner, he discussed the arrangements for the duel with Nesvitski, who was Pierre's second. Pierre went home, but Rostov, Dolokhov, and Denisov stayed on at the club until late, listening to the gypsy singers and other performers.
"So then — tomorrow at Sokolniki," said Dolokhov, taking leave of Rostov at the club entrance.
"And you feel completely calm?" Rostov asked.
Dolokhov paused.

"I'll tell you the whole secret of dueling in two words. If you're going to fight a duel and you sit down to write your will and tender letters to your parents, thinking you might be killed — you're a fool and you're done for. But if you go with the firm intention of killing your opponent as quickly and surely as possible, then everything will be fine. That's what our bear hunter back in Kostroma used to tell me: 'Everyone's afraid of a bear,' he'd say, 'but once you see one, all your fear vanishes — your only thought is not to let him get away!' That's how it is with me. [speaking in French] Till tomorrow, my dear fellow."
* Till tomorrow, my dear fellow.

The next morning, at eight o'clock, Pierre and Nesvitski drove to the Sokolniki forest, where they found Dolokhov, Denisov, and Rostov already waiting. Pierre had the look of a man consumed by thoughts that had nothing to do with the matter at hand. His drawn face was sallow. He had obviously not slept. He kept looking around distractedly and squinting as if dazzled by the sun. He was entirely preoccupied with two thoughts: his wife's guilt, of which he no longer had the slightest doubt after his sleepless night, and the blamelessness of Dolokhov, who had no reason to protect the honor of a man who meant nothing to him. "I would probably have done the same in his place," Pierre thought. "Actually, I'm sure I would have. So why this duel? Why this killing? Either I'll kill him, or he'll hit me in the head, or the elbow, or the knee. Why can't I just leave — run away — disappear somewhere?" Such thoughts kept passing through his mind. But at those very moments he would ask, in a particularly calm, distracted tone that earned the respect of the onlookers, "Will this take much longer? Is everything ready?"
When everything was prepared — the sabers planted in the snow to mark the barriers and the pistols loaded — Nesvitski walked up to Pierre.

"I would not be doing my duty, Count," he said in a timid voice, "and would not deserve the confidence and honor you've shown me by choosing me as your second, if at this grave — this very grave — moment, I did not tell you the whole truth. I believe there are no sufficient grounds for this affair, and no reason for blood to be shed. You were not entirely right — you were impulsive..."
"Oh yes, it's horribly stupid," said Pierre.

"Then allow me to convey your regrets, and I'm sure your opponent will accept them," said Nesvitski, who, like everyone else involved — and like everyone in such situations — still couldn't quite believe it had come to an actual duel. "You know, Count, it's far more honorable to admit a mistake than to let things become irreparable. There was no real insult on either side. Let me speak to them..."
"No! What is there to discuss?" said Pierre. "It doesn't matter.... Is everything ready?" he added. "Just tell me where to stand and where to aim." He said this with an unnaturally gentle smile.
He took the pistol and began asking how the trigger worked, since he had never held a pistol before — a fact he didn't want to admit.
"Oh yes, that's right — I know. I just forgot," he said.
"No apologies — none whatsoever," said Dolokhov to Denisov, who had been attempting a reconciliation on his side. Then Dolokhov too walked to his appointed place.

The spot chosen for the duel was about eighty paces from the road where the sleighs had been left — a small clearing in the pine forest, covered in melting snow, the frost having broken during the past few days. The two men stood forty paces apart at the far edge of the clearing. The seconds paced out the distance, leaving tracks in the deep, wet snow between the starting positions and the two sabers stuck in the ground ten paces apart to mark the barriers. The air was damp and misty. At forty paces, nothing could be seen clearly. For three minutes everything had been ready, but still they delayed, and everyone was silent.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter V
paragraphs: "Well, begin!" said Dolokhov.

"All right," said Pierre, still wearing that same strange smile. A sense of dread hung in the air. It was clear that what had begun so lightly could no longer be stopped — it was now taking its course, beyond anyone's control.
Denisov went first to the barrier and announced: "Since the adversaries have refused a reconciliation, please proceed. Take your pistols, and at the word 'three,' begin to advance."
"O-one! T-two! Three!" he shouted angrily, and stepped aside.

The two men advanced along the trampled paths, drawing nearer to each other and beginning to make out each other's forms through the mist. They had the right to fire whenever they chose as they approached the barrier. Dolokhov walked slowly, not raising his pistol, his bright, sparkling blue eyes fixed on his opponent's face. His mouth wore its usual hint of a smile.

"I can fire whenever I want!" said Pierre, and at the word "three" he strode quickly forward, missing the trodden path and stepping into the deep snow. He held the pistol in his outstretched right hand, apparently afraid of shooting himself with it. His left hand he held carefully back, wanting to use it to steady his right but knowing he wasn't supposed to. Having advanced six paces and wandered off the track into the snow, Pierre glanced down at his feet, then quickly looked up at Dolokhov, and bending his finger as he'd been shown, fired. Not at all expecting such a loud report, Pierre flinched at the sound, then stood still, smiling at his own reaction. The smoke, thickened by the mist, blocked his view for a moment, and there was no answering shot as he had expected. He only heard Dolokhov's hurried footsteps, and then a figure appeared through the smoke. Dolokhov was pressing one hand to his left side while the other clutched his sagging pistol. His face was white. Rostov ran toward him and said something.

"No-o-o!" Dolokhov muttered through clenched teeth. "No, it's not over." And after a few staggering steps toward the saber marking the barrier, he collapsed in the snow beside it. His left hand was bloody. He wiped it on his coat, then used it to prop himself up. His pale face was twisted in a grimace, trembling.
"Plea—" Dolokhov started, but couldn't get the word out.
"Please," he managed with an effort.
Pierre, barely holding back his sobs, began running toward Dolokhov and was about to cross the space between the barriers when Dolokhov shouted:

"Back to your barrier!" Pierre understood what he meant and stopped by his saber. Only ten paces separated them. Dolokhov lowered his head to the snow, bit at it greedily, then raised his head again, adjusted his position, drew in his legs, and sat up, trying to find his balance. He sucked at the cold snow and swallowed it. His lips quivered, but his eyes — still with that smile — glittered with effort and fury as he gathered his remaining strength. He raised his pistol and took aim.
"Sideways! Shield yourself with your pistol!" shouted Nesvitski.
"Cover yourself!" Even Denisov shouted to his opponent.

Pierre, with a gentle smile of pity and remorse, his arms and legs spread helplessly, stood with his broad chest fully exposed to Dolokhov and looked at him with sorrow. Denisov, Rostov, and Nesvitski squeezed their eyes shut. At the same instant they heard a shot and Dolokhov's furious cry.
"Missed!" Dolokhov shouted, and collapsed face-down in the snow, motionless.
Pierre clutched his temples, turned, and stumbled into the forest, plowing through the deep snow and muttering incoherent words.
"Madness... madness! Death... lies..." he repeated, his face contorted.
Nesvitski caught up with him and took him home.
Rostov and Denisov drove off with the wounded Dolokhov.

Dolokhov lay silent in the sleigh with his eyes closed, not answering any of the questions put to him. But as they entered Moscow, he suddenly came to, and lifting his head with effort, seized Rostov's hand. Rostov was struck by the completely transformed expression on Dolokhov's face — unexpectedly tender and full of anguish.
"How do you feel?" he asked.

"It's bad! But that's not what matters, my friend—" said Dolokhov in a gasping voice. "Where are we? In Moscow, I know. I don't matter, but I've killed her — killed her... She won't survive this! She won't survive..."
"Who?" asked Rostov.
"My mother! My mother — my angel, my precious, adored mother," said Dolokhov, and he pressed Rostov's hand and burst into tears.
When he had calmed down a little, he explained to Rostov that he lived with his mother, and that if she saw him dying, she would not survive it. He begged Rostov to go ahead and prepare her.

Rostov went ahead as asked, and to his great surprise he learned that Dolokhov the brawler, Dolokhov the thug, lived in Moscow with an elderly mother and a hunchbacked sister, and was the most loving and devoted of sons and brothers.
